lead: When a system has more than one CPU core and some tasks must meet strict deadlines, the scheduler must decide not only which ready thread runs next, but also on which core it runs and whether the timing guarantees can be met. Multiprocessor load‑balancing, CPU affinity, and real‑time algorithms such as Rate‑Monotonic (RM) and Earliest‑Deadline‑First (EDF) provide the mechanisms to keep all cores busy while respecting hard or soft timing constraints. These techniques are used in smartphones handling UI threads, in servers running parallel services, and in embedded controllers of trains or medical devices.
prereq: You need: basic process and thread concepts from 2.1, thread basics from 2.5, and scheduling criteria from 2.6.

sections.h3: Multiprocessor load balancing and CPU affinity

blocks.text: A multiprocessor system has several identical CPUs that share main memory. The scheduler keeps a run‑queue for each CPU. When a thread becomes ready, it is placed on one of these queues. Load balancing moves threads between queues so that no CPU stays idle while another is overloaded.

items: Per‑CPU run‑queue reduces lock contention.
Load‑balancer runs periodically (e.g., every 10 ms) and migrates tasks.
CPU affinity remembers the last CPU a thread ran on; keeping it there improves cache reuse.
A strong affinity flag is a scheduler hint that a thread should stay on its preferred CPU unless the system is severely imbalanced.
Thread becomes runnable → add to local run‑queue.
Scheduler picks the highest‑priority thread from its queue.
If the queue is empty, the balancer searches other CPUs and pulls a task.
If a thread has a strong affinity flag, it is kept on its preferred CPU unless the system is heavily imbalanced.

blocks.where: L_i is the number of runnable threads on CPU i; avg(L_i) is the average over all CPUs.

blocks.text: Real‑time tasks have a period T (time between releases) and a worst‑case execution time C. Utilization U = C/T expresses the fraction of CPU time a task needs. For a set of n independent periodic tasks, the total utilization is Σ C_i/T_i.

items: Hard real‑time: missing a deadline can cause system failure (e.g., airbag deployment).
Soft real‑time: occasional deadline miss degrades quality (e.g., video playback).
Jitter = variation in actual start time of a periodic job.
Compute U for each task.
Add them to get U_total.
If using EDF, check U_total ≤ 1.

If using RM, compare U_total with the Liu‑Layland bound. If U_total ≤ bound, RM guarantees that all deadlines are met. If U_total > bound, the test is inconclusive – the task set may still be feasible, and a more detailed analysis (e.g., response‑time analysis) is required.

blocks.where: n is the number of tasks; bound is the maximum utilization for which Rate‑Monotonic scheduling guarantees all deadlines.

blocks.code:
import math
n=3
bound = n*(2**(1/n)-1)
print(f"RM bound = {bound:.3f}")

blocks.text: EDF is optimal for uniprocessor systems: if any algorithm can meet all deadlines, EDF can. It dynamically orders jobs by earliest absolute deadline. RM is a static priority scheme; tasks with shorter periods get higher priority. RM is easier to implement on small microcontrollers because priorities never change at run time.

items: Use EDF when total utilization is close to 1 and tasks have varying periods.
Use RM for low‑cost embedded devices with a small, fixed set of periodic tasks.
For multiprocessor systems, partitioned scheduling assigns each task to a single CPU and runs the chosen uniprocessor algorithm per CPU.
List all tasks with C and T.
Compute U_total.
If U_total ≤ 1 → EDF feasible.
If U_total ≤ RM bound → RM is guaranteed feasible. If U_total > RM bound, the test is inconclusive; the task set may still be schedulable with more detailed analysis.
Otherwise, consider task splitting or a hybrid algorithm.

examples.question: Three periodic tasks are defined as follows: Task A has C = 1 ms, T = 5 ms; Task B has C = 2 ms, T = 10 ms; Task C has C = 2 ms, T = 20 ms. Determine whether the task set is schedulable under EDF and under RM.
steps: Compute utilization of each task: U_A = 1/5 = 0.2, U_B = 2/10 = 0.2, U_C = 2/20 = 0.1.
For EDF, check U_total ≤ 1 → 0.5 ≤ 1, so EDF can meet all deadlines.
For RM, n = 3 tasks. Compute RM bound = 3 × (2^{1/3} – 1) ≈ 0.779.
Since U_total = 0.5 ≤ 0.779, RM also guarantees all deadlines.
examples.answer: The task set is schedulable under both EDF and Rate‑Monotonic scheduling.
examples.check:
U_A = 1/5
U_B = 2/10
U_C = 2/20
U_total = U_A + U_B + U_C
import math
rm_bound = 3 * (2**(1/3) - 1)
print(round(U_total,3))
print(round(rm_bound,3))

traps: Treating the utilization bound for RM as 1; the bound is lower for more than one task.
Ignoring context‑switch overhead when adding utilizations; the real U_total is slightly higher.
Assuming EDF works unchanged on multiprocessor systems without partitioning; migration can invalidate the simple U ≤ 1 test.
Confusing period T with deadline D; a task may have D < T, which changes feasibility checks.

quiz.q: What is CPU affinity in a multiprocessor scheduler?
quiz.a: A hint that a thread prefers to run on the same CPU where it last executed, improving cache reuse.

quiz.q: Explain why a per‑CPU run‑queue reduces lock contention.
quiz.a: Each CPU accesses only its own queue, so threads do not need to acquire a global lock when enqueuing or dequeuing.

quiz.q: Given three tasks with (C,T) = (1,4), (2,5), (1,10), compute the total utilization and decide if EDF can schedule them.
quiz.a: U = 1/4 + 2/5 + 1/10 = 0.25 + 0.4 + 0.1 = 0.75 ≤ 1, so EDF can meet all deadlines.

quiz.q: A system has four CPUs with run‑queue lengths [3,7,2,5]. Compute the load imbalance ratio.
Why might a hard‑real‑time task be assigned a higher static priority than a soft‑real‑time task even if its period is longer?
quiz.a: Because missing the hard deadline could cause catastrophic failure, the scheduler must guarantee its execution, outweighing the shorter period of the soft task.

quiz.q: A set of four periodic tasks has total utilization 0.92. Under RM the Liu‑Layland bound is 0.756. What can you conclude?
quiz.a: RM cannot guarantee all deadlines, but the set may still be feasible with EDF or with a more advanced multiprocessor algorithm.

quiz.q: Define jitter in the context of real‑time scheduling.
quiz.a: Jitter is the variation in the actual start time of a periodic job relative to its expected release time.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, real‑time schedulers are integrated into automotive AUTOSAR stacks and aerospace DO‑178C certified software. Research explores mixed‑criticality systems where high‑criticality tasks receive stronger guarantees than low‑criticality ones. Emerging heterogeneous platforms combine big‑LITTLE cores, requiring new affinity and deadline‑aware load‑balancing policies. Cloud providers also use deadline‑aware scheduling for latency‑sensitive services. To go deeper, look for papers on partitioned vs. global multiprocessor real‑time scheduling and on the Linux SCHED_DEADLINE API.
